own_scenes.desc: En mayo de 2000 Pop Culture Media y Carol Marvin, organizadora de los festivales de jazz, montaron el primer Detroit Electronic Music Festival, gratis, en Hart Plaza, con Carl Craig como director artístico. Al caer el sol del primer sábado, con el set de Stacey Pullen, la plaza estaba llena: la ciudad se reencontraba con su niño prodigio, Detroit por fin «entendía» el techno. (Se habló de un millón y medio de asistentes, cifra imposible.) En 2001 Marvin despidió a Craig justo antes del festival; él perdió la demanda pero ganó el voto popular («DEMF = Carl Craig»). Sobrevivió a tres cambios de dirección: Saunderson lo llevó en 2005 (Fuse-In) y dimitió, y en 2006 la ciudad se lo dio a Paxahau, que comprobó que el aforo de Hart Plaza era de 45.000 personas, cuidó el sonido y lo convirtió, con entrada de pago, en Movement, algo con lo que Detroit puede contar cada año. El techno ha perdido su misterio, pero la credibilidad de Detroit ya desborda sus calles.

refs.q: Detroit finally “got” techno—it was emotional, magical, and as hyperbolic as you might imagine.
refs.para: When the sun set on the first Saturday, enthusiasts, suburban visitors, city residents, and random passersby flocked to the free festival, converging on Stacey Pullen’s DJ set on the main stage. Hart Plaza was at or near capacity. The weather was perfect. Downtown Detroit came alive with strange, yet familiar sounds. What everyone slowly realized was that they were witnessing and participating in the reunion of the city with its long-lost, homegrown Wunderkind. Detroit finally “got” techno—it was emotional, magical, and as hyperbolic as you might imagine.
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: Applied Technology: The Myth of Techno Collides with Reality, 1991–2001

refs.q: “Even with all the politics and all the bullshit—the typical Detroit politics—I would never change it,” said Craig. “It was great.”
refs.para: The following year brought with it a new plot development. Though she had chosen Carl Craig to act as “artistic director” of the festival in 2000, Carol Marvin decided to fire him just before the opening day of the second DEMF. Marvin cited that Craig did not fulfill the terms of his contract, and Craig in turn sued (and lost) for defamation of character and breach of contract. But Craig seemed to have won “the popular vote,” as banners and stickers bearing the slogans “I Support Carl Craig” and “DEMF = Carl Craig” were visible all weekend. And, to this day, the artistic direction and lineups of the first two festivals are regarded by many as the best. “Even with all the politics and all the bullshit—the typical Detroit politics—I would never change it,” said Craig. “It was great.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: Applied Technology: The Myth of Techno Collides with Reality, 1991–2001

refs.q: The result is that Detroit’s street cred has become much larger than the boundaries of its streets.
refs.para: For better or worse, techno has shed a lot of its mystique. There are no secret identities left to uncover, fewer hidden messages tucked in the run-out grooves. And now, party promoters who once searched for out-of-the-way venues and buildings are now out in the open. Moreover, techno has been documented and celebrated on many levels by this point. The result is that Detroit’s street cred has become much larger than the boundaries of its streets.
